balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For James Hardie Industries plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For James Hardie Industries plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For James Hardie Industries plc: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For James Hardie Industries plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

asbestos.title: AICF asbestos liability and cash payments
asbestos.content:
James Hardie manufactured asbestos-containing products in Australia until 1987. Under a 2007 deed with the Australian government, compensation for current and future claims is channelled through the Asbestos Injuries Compensation Fund (AICF), a trust legally separate from James Hardie's operating business. James Hardie funds it each year under a formula equal to roughly 35% of free cash flow (subject to an annual cap, with any shortfall carried to later years), capped around 1-2% of group revenue in most years. Claims paid is cash AICF pays to claimants; cash paid to AICF is James Hardie's annual funding transfer; the liability is the actuarially estimated present value of all future claims still on the balance sheet.

For James Hardie Industries plc: this is non-recourse to operating assets and capped by formula, so it will not bankrupt the company -- but it is a real, contractual, FCF-linked cash outflow every year, not a one-off provision. The DCF's owner FCF should be read alongside this chart, not independently of it.

What to watch:

  • The liability re-estimate (periodic actuarial reviews can move it materially in either direction)
  • Cash paid to AICF rising in step with FCF under the funding formula
  • Any sign the formula or cap is renegotiated

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue mix
segmentRevenue.content:
James Hardie reports three segments: North America Fiber Cement (siding and trim, the large majority of revenue and profit), Asia Pacific Fiber Cement (Australia, New Zealand, Philippines) and Europe Building Products (Fermacell, fiber-gypsum building panels, acquired 2018).

For James Hardie Industries plc: in August 2026 James Hardie agreed to divest Europe Building Products to Holcim. The segment split only reaches the Metrics CSV from FY2022 (earlier filings did not break it out at this granularity), so the chart is short but it is the only view that shows how small and separable Europe always was next to North America.

What to watch:

  • North America's share of the mix growing as Europe is divested
  • Asia Pacific as the smaller, more cyclical growth segment relative to North America's scale
  • Post-divestiture: Revenue and EBITDA levels should be read against the smaller continuing-operations base, not the historical consolidated totals above

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For James Hardie Industries plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
